title: Positive Manifold Visualiser
summary: Six fictional cognitive tasks and a correlation matrix students control by deciding how much of each task's performance is shared with all tasks, shared within a group, or specific and error. Scatterplots, a loading diagram and a genuinely computed first factor follow — and the same positive first factor appears whether the structure underneath is one general ability or two groups.
learningObjectives: State the positive manifold as an empirical pattern rather than as a theory.
Explain why a first factor with positive loadings follows arithmetically from an all-positive correlation matrix.
Recognise that a general factor and broad group factors produce similar first-factor loadings.
Distinguish shared, group, task-specific and error variance and say which of them can contribute to a correlation.
Name rival explanations of the positive manifold and what evidence would be needed to choose between them.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges and buttons; sliders announce meaningful values such as '55% shared by every task'. Every correlation-matrix cell prints its own number so the shading is redundant, and same-group pairs carry a border as well as a tint. The variance bar prints each segment's name and percentage inside it. Scatterplots and the loading chart are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables giving model-implied and observed correlations and every loading, with group membership stated in its own column rather than by bar colour. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: The positive manifold: an empirical pattern, the first factor that follows from it, and why extracting one settles nothing
simulationNotes: Six fictional cognitive tasks in two groups. Each task score is a weighted sum of a general source, a group source, a task-specific source and error, all independent standard normal and scaled to unit variance, so the model-implied correlation is g-squared plus group-squared for same-group pairs. Scatterplots use 220 simulated people from a seeded mulberry32 generator. The first factor is genuinely computed by the power method on the matrix shown, reported as eigenvector times the square root of the eigenvalue, with variance explained as eigenvalue over number of tasks. No real intelligence test, subtest, item, norm or published correlation matrix is reproduced, no ability score is produced for anyone, and the tool contains one undifferentiated population so can support no claim about differences between groups of people. A factor here is described throughout as a property of a correlation matrix and never as a biological entity.
